steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The sea had a way of erasing things—footprints in the sand, names on hulls, even time itself. But it had not yet managed to erase Elias Finn.

For twenty-nine years, Elias had kept the lamp at Harrow’s Reach Lighthouse alive. Every evening, just after the horizon bruised purple, he’d climb the iron spiral, oil the gears, polish the lens, and coax the lantern into an amber bloom that swept across the waves. That light, he liked to believe, stitched a thin, gleaming thread between him and every sailor who trusted the dark.

One March night the wind arrived early, rattling the shutters before dusk. The island’s only radio fizzed, hissed, and surrendered to static. Squalls weren’t unusual, but something inside the storm felt different—hurried, almost purposeful. As he lit the lamp, Elias noticed the beam faltering, catching for a breath before regaining its swing. He tapped the housing. Again, the light blinked. Impossible; he’d serviced it that morning.

Outside, surf pounded the rocks like a war drum. When lightning split the sky, Elias thought he saw a silhouette caught on the cliffs: a woman, shawl whipping, hand raised not in panic but in greeting. The next flash revealed only spindrift.

He descended, lantern in hand, and trudged into the gale. The wind stole his name when he shouted. Nothing answered but the roaring dark. Yet on the ground, half-buried in sea grass, lay a brass spyglass—antique, its leather wrapping worn smooth. He ran a thumb over the initials engraved at the base: M.F.

His mother, Marion Finn, had carried such a spyglass the night her fishing boat vanished, thirty years ago.

Elias returned to the tower, heart hammering like loose rigging. The beacon flickered once more, then steadied the instant he set the spyglass beside it—as though the two machines recognized each other. Drawn by impulse, he lifted the glass to his eye, aiming not at the water but at the distance between stars. Through it he saw a vessel trimmed in moon-white sails, gliding a sky-blue current. On the deck stood his mother, smiling, her hand raised exactly as before.

The beam swung, grazing her ethereal hull, and Elias understood: some ships no longer sailed the ocean but the in-between, and even there they sought safe passage. He kept the glass to his eye until dawn paled the heavens and the vision faded like chalk in rain.

The lighthouse never faltered again. Sailors spoke of an uncanny guiding glow that seemed to widen, as if searching, generous beyond duty. And on clear nights, when stars swarmed the sky like fireflies adrift, Elias Finn stood watch, the spyglass warm in his palm, lighting the way for travelers on every tide he could reach—those of water, those of wind, and those of memory.
